title: Kickstarting an Emergency
html:
I have been a big fan of projects like Kiva.org originating from when some of my relatives started giving money through its services to people around the world a few years back. And Kickstarter’s approach to funding projects has been inspiring to follow. Although micro-credit is not new (Johnathan Swift created the Irish Load Fund System in the 18th century as one of the first formal systems and more recently people have become aware of Muhammad Yunus’ philanthropic endeavor - the Grameen Bank), what inspires me about the new solutions is how modern technology is enabling effective crowd-sourced funding.

I have often wondered how we could apply a similar approach to disaster response, but generally got held back when thinking about all the logistical, verification, and trust-worthy issues. I have brainstormed the idea with many people, but we always keep getting “bogged down in the weeds”. Recently, I realized that it was perhaps because we keep thinking of starting the concept from scratch rather than transforming funding mechanisms that already exist. As Global Humanitarian Assistance points out, there are different ways that humanitarian financing is channeled “through the UN system, an international or local NGO, the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement or through the affected government institutions”. However, what strikes me is that there is no easy way for compassionate individuals to give directly to the affected population. Could we modify one of these mechanisms to be a modern, tech-enabled disaster response fund aimed at local individuals?

In recent books by Steven Johnson and Eric Schmidt, they both propose the idea of a Kickstarter-like fund for emergencies. But, they both raise a core reason why they believe it could not be done - trust. How can we trust who is asking for funding? And how we can ensure the most in-need are the ones being heard when it is the more wealthy who have the money to buy gadgets? However, it was a point that Johnson raised in another context that made me realize: why not modify something that already exists to look and function more like Kickstarter or Kiva? Why not modify the UN’s Humanitarian pooled funds to have elements that work in this way? Could we make the UN-OCHA’s managed Common Humanitarian Fund / Emergency Response Fund look like a Kickstarter? These local funds would allow for management by those who understand the local context and have relationships with NGOs, Government agencies, camps, communities or other groups that could provide monitoring services. We could establish pre-disaster relationships to build out a sort-of trusted network of individuals or community leaders who could rapidly verify identities. It could be part of a larger resilience network especially if we provided the technology (e.g. smart phones) both in advance and directly after the crisis to enable affected community to appeal for help. This network would enable the trust needed and would provide the monitoring desired by those who give. Diaspora networks could also be tapped in order to help with verification and monitoring. And, if unaffected local populations were supporting their fellow citizen through the fund, they may need less ‘verification’ or trust before giving money.

Hopefully others would also adopt a similar approach. Governments could start their own funding mechanism which could adhere to a yet undefined international standards. They have even better local knowledge. Of course, in some countries that knowledge could be used in a very impartial or inappropriate way so oversight and safety would need to be paramount.

So, if we were to take an existing funding mechanism and modify it, what are some of the features could it have?

  1. Crowd-funding. Allowing the affected to appeal as individuals or groups to the world for direct funding would enable the affected to ask for exactly what they need and would allow others to give specifically to those they want. Technological options like Kiva and Kickstarter bring important elements and processes, but others such as HopeMob provide important services such as being fee-free, being open to all people and causes, undertaking story verification, and writing stories on the requester’s behalf.
  2. Lending. By providing a platform where people could specify their need and neighbors responding with the ability to give or lend a solution could be massive. Effectively this approach would enable participatory aid. Peerby is an example of a local lending app that gives neighbors the ability to participate in the sharing economy. Airbnb opened its service during Hurricane Sandy and has since launched a Disaster Response program. By connecting such tools to a central service, it could help enforce standards (e.g. amount of water that is needed by one person) and provide a more clear picture of overall remaining needs.
  3. Investing. Rather than just giving money, people are often keen to invest in something more sustainable than sort-term relief. Perhaps we could enable the ability to invest in people. Pave lets prospects appeal for financial support to improve themselves or their ideas. They are looking for backers who will invest in their career. Perhaps in an emergency situation, the affected would need to articulate how they are going to use the money to alleviate their suffering AND how they will use it to improve in the long term. This approach would be be mixing disaster response with development.

Is there really a need?

One common question I receive is about the real need for such a solution given the number of funds we already have. Other than streamlining aid flow directly to the affected and having no theoretical upper-limit in terms of amount for a given emergency, one reason that I believe such a fund would be beneficial is the lack of credit in the world. It is often those affected by disaster who need money quickly. According to Michael Saylor in The Mobile Wave: How Mobile Intelligence Will Change Everything the “third World is a credit desert. Worldwide, 53 percent of adults are unbanked. They lie outside the formal financial system. The highest rate is 80 percent of adults - 326 million - in sub-Saharan Africa. But there are also 67% in Middle East, 59% in East Asia, 65% in Latin America, and 58% in South East Asia”. These are the people who are often the ones most affected in a crisis. And when these people need loans, “they rely on informal sources like friends, money lenders, shopkeepers, and landlords.” Saylor highlights one study that found “the poor borrowed just 6 percent of their funds from formal sources like banks…..most of the rest of the money came from informal sources” and cited an example of typical, informal interest rates in Hyderabad, India being 57%.

Imagine if we could provide the affected with technology that enabled them to support each other, appeal for financial assistance or ask for lost-cost external funding when needed. A Kickstarter-like funding mechanism married with digital currencies, mobile banking (e.g M-Pesa), and other tech-enabled services (e.g. AidBox, 3D printing, Humanitarian Conceigre, etc.) could reduce significant amounts of “friction” from the lives of those affected by disasters. It would help to turn humanitarianism into a service and would reshape the function of the UN/NGOs to serve more as aggregators than top-down directors.

So, my answers is: Yes such a solution is needed. Of course bringing such a solution to reality will require significant open-mindedness, collaboration and time, but I believe that it would be well worth the effort.

Andrej

teaser: The case that a crowdfunding solution for emergencies is needed, with community verification and diaspora networks, inspired by Kiva and Kickstarter.
seo_description: Why a Kickstarter-like service for emergencies is needed, how trust and verification might work, and what it would take to make it real.
